claim: Presynaptic G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) locally influence synaptic strength and can operate on a wide range of time scales.
source: Presynaptic G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) are critical in this problem as they locally influence synaptic strength and can operate on a wide range of time scales.
evidence: This is a general statement about GPCR function that draws from established scientific understanding of these receptors.

claim: GPCRs impact neurotransmission by inhibiting voltage-gated calcium (Ca2+) influx in the active zone.
source: Among the mechanisms by which GPCRs impact neurotransmission is by inhibiting voltage-gated calcium (Ca2+) influx in the active zone.
evidence: This is a known mechanism of GPCR action supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: There is an unexpected non-linear relationship between the magnitude of action potential driven Ca2+ influx and the concentration of external Ca2+ ([Ca2+]e).
source: Here, using quantitative analysis of both single bouton Ca2+ influx and exocytosis, we uncovered an unexpected non-linear relationship between the magnitude of action potential driven Ca2+ influx and the concentration of external Ca2+ ([Ca2+]e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements using physin-GCaMP6f shown in Figure 1.

claim: GPCR signaling operating at the nominal physiological set point for [Ca2+]e (1.2 mM) can achieve complete silencing of nerve terminals.
source: We find that this unexpected relationship is leveraged by GPCR signaling when operating at the nominal physiological set point for [Ca2+]e, 1.2 mM, to achieve complete silencing of nerve terminals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing baclofen-induced silencing at physiological [Ca2+]e shown in Figure 7.

claim: Information throughput in neural circuits can be readily modulated in an all-or-none fashion at the single synapse level when operating at the physiological set point.
source: These data imply that the information throughput in neural circuits can be readily modulated in an all-or-none fashion at the single synapse level when operating at the physiological set point.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of terminal silencing.

claim: A canonical mode of presynaptic modulation occurs via the binding of voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) by G-protein βγ subunits after they dissociate from the trimeric G-protein complex following GPCR activation.
source: A canonical mode of presynaptic modulation occurs via the binding of voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) by G-protein βγ subunits after they dissociate from the trimeric G-protein complex following GPCR activation (Herlitze et al., 1996).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Herlitze et al., 1996.

claim: GPCR-mediated inhibition of VGCCs impacts neurotransmission.
source: The impact of GPCR-mediated inhibition of VGCCs on neurotransmission (Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000; Yamada et al., 1999) is amplified by the exquisite sensitivity of exocytosis to the magnitude of Ca2+ influx, which underlies the ability to rapidly change exocytotic rates at sites of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000 and Yamada et al., 1999.

claim: The sensitivity of exocytosis to Ca2+ influx is driven by the cooperative binding of multiple Ca2+ ions to one or more Ca2+ sensors that form core elements of the exocytic machinery.
source: This sensitivity is driven by the cooperative binding of multiple Ca2+ ions to one or more Ca2+ sensors that form core elements of the exocytic machinery (Heidelberger et al., 1994; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000; Bollmann et al., 2000; Ariel and Ryan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating cooperative Ca2+ binding.

claim: Modifying the open probability of VGCCs serves as a potent means of presynaptic control, as small changes in Ca2+ influx can lead to large changes in neurotransmitter release.
source: Modifying the open probability of VGCCs, therefore, serves as a potent means of presynaptic control, as small changes in Ca2+ influx can lead to large changes in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cooperative nature of Ca2+ binding to exocytic machinery.

claim: The impact of Ca2+ on exocytosis depends on local changes in Ca2+ concentration near the active zone, which in turn depend on the external Ca2+ concentration bathing the nerve terminal.
source: The impact of Ca2+ on exocytosis depends on local changes in Ca2+ concentration near the active zone, which in turn depend on the external Ca2+ concentration bathing the nerve terminal (Dittman and Ryan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dittman and Ryan, 2019.

claim: The steepness of the relationship between exocytosis rates and Ca2+ influx depends crucially on resting [Ca2+]e.
source: Thus, the steepness of the relationship between exocytosis rates and Ca2+ influx depends crucially on resting [Ca2+]e.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dependence of local Ca2+ concentration on external Ca2+ concentration.

claim: Plasma [Ca2+] is strictly regulated in vivo.
source: In vivo, plasma [Ca2+] is strictly regulated, and the CNS is very sensitive to plasma [Ca2+] perturbations, with seizures precipitated by hypocalcemia and psychiatric symptoms progressing to lethargy or coma with worsening hypercalcemia (Riggs, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riggs, 2002.

claim: The CNS is very sensitive to plasma [Ca2+] perturbations, with seizures precipitated by hypocalcemia and psychiatric symptoms progressing to lethargy or coma with worsening hypercalcemia.
source: In vivo, plasma [Ca2+] is strictly regulated, and the CNS is very sensitive to plasma [Ca2+] perturbations, with seizures precipitated by hypocalcemia and psychiatric symptoms progressing to lethargy or coma with worsening hypercalcemia (Riggs, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riggs, 2002.

claim: Feedback loops controlled by Ca2+ sensors of the parathyroid gland act to maintain plasma [Ca2+] at a set point of 1.2 mM in most mammals.
source: Feedback loops controlled by Ca2+ sensors of the parathyroid gland act to maintain plasma [Ca2+] at a set point of 1.2 mM in most mammals (Hannan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hannan et al., 2019.

claim: Previous studies investigating the dependency of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e in nerve terminals of the CNS found the relationship obeyed a simple saturable pore model with a Kd of [Ca2+]e ~2.5 mM.
source: Previous studies investigating the dependency of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e in nerve terminals of the CNS found the relationship obeyed a simple saturable pore model with a Kd of [Ca2+]e ~2.5 mM (Ariel and Ryan, 2010; Schneggenburger et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ariel and Ryan, 2010 and Schneggenburger et al., 1999.

claim: The simple saturable pore model predicts that changes in Δ[Ca2+]i will exhibit 1-to-1 proportionality to [Ca2+]e at concentrations well below Kd.
source: This model predicts that changes in Δ[Ca2+]i will exhibit 1-to-1 proportionality to [Ca2+]e at concentrations well below Kd, which is substantially higher than the physiologic set point ([Ca2+]e = 1.2 mM).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the saturable pore model.

claim: Previous measurements of the relationship between Δ[Ca2+]i and [Ca2+]e were not carried out at physiological temperatures.
source: One important confound, however, is that previous measurements were not carried out at physiological temperatures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: At 37°C, there is a sub-proportional relationship of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e as the concentration was lowered below 2.0 mM.
source: Here, where the temperature was set to 37 °C, we observed an unexpected sub-proportional relationship of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e as the concentration was lowered below 2.0 mM (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The magnitude of difference between the expected and experimentally measured Δ[Ca2+]i was greater at [Ca2+]e 0.8 mM compared to 1.2 mM.
source: The magnitude of difference between the expected and experimentally measured Δ[Ca2+]i was greater at [Ca2+]e 0.8 mM compared to 1.2 mM, highlighting that this discrepancy manifests most prominently below the set point (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A linear extrapolation from the mean Δ[Ca2+]i measurements relative to [Ca2+]e predicts the cessation of Ca2+ entry into nerve terminals at [Ca2+]e of 0.47 mM.
source: A linear extrapolation from the mean Δ[Ca2+]i measurements relative to [Ca2+]e predicts the cessation of Ca2+ entry into nerve terminals at [Ca2+]e of 0.47 mM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on linear extrapolation of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At [Ca2+]e = 0.4 mM, there is almost no measurable residual Ca2+ influx (estimated Δ[Ca2+]~1.6 nM).
source: Experiments carried out using [Ca2+]e = 0.4 mM confirm that there is almost no measurable residual Ca2+ influx under these conditions (estimated Δ[Ca2+]~1.6 nM; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), far below the value expected (10.4 nM) if Ca2+ influx obeyed a simple linear proportionality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of terminals exhibited an all-or-none response to lowering [Ca2+]e below the physiologic set point such that Δ[Ca2+]i is selectively abolished.
source: Surprisingly, we found that a subset of terminals exhibited an all-or-none response to lowering [Ca2+]e below the physiologic set point such that Δ[Ca2+]i is selectively abolished (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Silencing occurred despite robust Δ[Ca2+]i at higher [Ca2+]e and even if synaptic neighbors of a terminal exhibited persistent Ca2+ entry at a lower concentration.
source: We observed that silencing occurred despite robust Δ[Ca2+]i at higher [Ca2+]e and even if synaptic neighbors of a terminal exhibited persistent Ca2+ entry at a lower concentration (Figure 2A and B), suggesting the impact of [Ca2+]e on neuronal function is exerted at the single synapse level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The impact of [Ca2+]e on neuronal function is exerted at the single synapse level.
source: We observed that silencing occurred despite robust Δ[Ca2+]i at higher [Ca2+]e and even if synaptic neighbors of a terminal exhibited persistent Ca2+ entry at a lower concentration (Figure 2A and B), suggesting the impact of [Ca2+]e on neuronal function is exerted at the single synapse level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that neighboring terminals can have different responses.

claim: Individual axonal branches have both silent and responding terminals.
source: These experiments showed that individual axonal branches have both silent and responding terminals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), indicating that branch point failure cannot account for [Ca2+]e mediated silencing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Branch point failure cannot account for [Ca2+]e mediated silencing.
source: These experiments showed that individual axonal branches have both silent and responding terminals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), indicating that branch point failure cannot account for [Ca2+]e mediated silencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that individual branches have both silent and responding terminals.

claim: There is substantial heterogeneity in the proportion of silent terminals across a population of neurons (coefficient of variation was 38%, 56%, and 57% for [Ca2+]e 0.8, 1.2, and 2.0 mM, respectively).
source: Across a population of neurons (Figure 3), we found substantial heterogeneity in the proportion of silent terminals (coefficient of variation was 38%, 56%, and 57% for [Ca2+]e 0.8, 1.2, and 2.0 mM, respectively) but a strikingly disproportionate increase in the mean proportion of silencing below 1.2 mM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a strikingly disproportionate increase in the mean proportion of silencing below 1.2 mM [Ca2+]e.
source: Across a population of neurons (Figure 3), we found substantial heterogeneity in the proportion of silent terminals (coefficient of variation was 38%, 56%, and 57% for [Ca2+]e 0.8, 1.2, and 2.0 mM, respectively) but a strikingly disproportionate increase in the mean proportion of silencing below 1.2 mM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The change in percentage of silencing versus change in [Ca2+]e was 48.9% mM–1 transitioning from 1.2 to 0.8 mM compared to 19.0% mM–1 from 2.0 to 1.2 mM.
source: The change in percentage of silencing versus change in [Ca2+]e was 48.9% mM–1 transitioning from 1.2 to 0.8 mM compared to 19.0% mM–1 from 2.0 to 1.2 mM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nearly all terminals (93%) are silent in [Ca2+]e 0.4 mM.
source: We separately tested the proportion of silencing when transitioning from 1.2 mM to 0.4 mM, observing that nearly all terminals (93%) are silent in [Ca2+]e 0.4 mM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: [Ca2+]e of 0.4 mM potently and consistently shuts down presynaptic function.
source: Here, the coefficient of variation, 5%, was substantially lower (32% in paired measurements in [Ca2+]e 1.2 mM), demonstrating this level of [Ca2+]e potently and consistently shuts down presynaptic function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low coefficient of variation and high proportion of silencing at 0.4 mM [Ca2+]e.

claim: The change in percentage of silencing versus change in [Ca2+]e transition between 0.8 mM to 0.4 mM is 73.3% mM–1.
source: The change in percentage of silencing versus change in [Ca2+]e transition between 0.8 mM to 0.4 mM is 73.3% mM–1, again highlighting the steep dependence of silencing on [Ca2+]e below the physiologic [Ca2+]e.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: Responding terminals demonstrated Δ[Ca2+]i that scaled with [Ca2+]e.
source: As expected, responding terminals demonstrated Δ[Ca2+]i that scaled with [Ca2+]e (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nerve terminal silencing was reversible as the proportion of silent terminals before and after switching [Ca2+]e from 2.0 mM to 0.8 mM was unchanged.
source: Nerve terminal silencing was reversible as the proportion of silent terminals before and after switching [Ca2+]e from 2.0 mM to 0.8 mM was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Ca2+ influx at hippocampal nerve terminals occurs predominantly via N- and P/Q-type VGCCs, with substantial heterogeneity between neurons in their proportional contribution to Ca2+ influx.
source: Ca2+ influx at hippocampal nerve terminals occurs predominantly via N- and P/Q-type VGCCs, with substantial heterogeneity between neurons in their proportional contribution to Ca2+ influx (Ariel et al., 2012; Ermolyuk et al., 2013; Hoppa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ariel et al., 2012; Ermolyuk et al., 2013; Hoppa et al., 2012.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) silences a subpopulation of nerve terminals, an effect mediated by N-type channels only.
source: Previously, cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) was shown to silence a subpopulation of nerve terminals, an effect mediated by N-type channels only (Kim and Ryan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim and Ryan, 2013.

claim: The contribution of presynaptic VGCC subtypes to Δ[Ca2+]i is variable between hippocampal neurons.
source: As previously demonstrated, the contribution of presynaptic VGCC subtypes to Δ[Ca2+]i is variable between hippocampal neurons (Figure 4B and C; Ariel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C and citation to Ariel et al., 2012.

claim: A subset of terminals is silenced with acute inhibition of either N-type or P/Q-type channels, but the isolation of N-type channels leads to greater proportions of silent terminals.
source: A subset of terminals is silenced with acute inhibition of either subtype, but the isolation of N-type channels leads to greater proportions of silent terminals (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Lowering of absolute Ca2+ influx steeply increases the fraction of silent terminals.
source: This analysis reveals a non-linear relationship, such that lowering of absolute Ca2+ influx steeply increases the fraction of silent terminals.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between Ca2+ entry and silencing shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The comparison of Δ[Ca2+]i to silencing was well described with a Hill equation (r2 = 0.99, Kd = 25 nM, n = –1.79) and closely matched the relationship observed without toxin application (r2 = 0.77, Kd = 23 nM, n = –1.46).
source: The comparison of Δ[Ca2+]i to silencing was well described with a Hill equation (r2 = 0.99, Kd = 25 nM, n = –1.79) and closely matched the relationship observed without toxin application (r2 = 0.77, Kd = 23 nM, n = –1.46; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on fitting experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The proportion of silent nerve terminals is critically related to global absolute Ca2+ influx and differences between N- and P/Q-type channels are driven primarily by the impact that acute inhibition has on Ca2+ entry.
source: This analysis indicates that the proportion of silent nerve terminals is critically related to global absolute Ca2+ influx and that differences between N- and P/Q-type channels are driven primarily by the impact that acute inhibition has on Ca2+ entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of the relationship between Ca2+ influx and silencing across different conditions.

claim: Silencing of SV recycling occurred at a substantial subset of nerve terminals (~25 to 55%).
source: Similar to synaptic Ca2+ influx, silencing of SV recycling occurred at a substantial subset of nerve terminals (~25 to 55%, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The proportion of silent terminals was heterogeneous across neurons but the mean and range at each [Ca2+]e were similar to the degree of silencing observed with Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: The proportion of silent terminals was heterogeneous across neurons but the mean and range at each [Ca2+]e were similar to the degree of silencing observed with Δ[Ca2+]i (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data from SV recycling and Ca2+ influx measurements.

claim: The increase in SV recycling in responding terminals scaled with [Ca2+]e.
source: As expected, the increase in SV recycling in responding terminals scaled with [Ca2+]e (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SV recycling is modulated in an all-or-none manner by modest changes in [Ca2+]e around the physiological set point ([Ca2+]e = 1.2 mM).
source: Thus, as with Ca2+ influx, SV recycling is modulated in an all-or-none manner by modest changes in [Ca2+]e around the physiological set point ([Ca2+]e = 1.2 mM).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of terminal silencing in SV recycling experiments.

claim: Glutamate exocytosis evoked by a single AP exhibited higher proportions of silencing at neurotransmitter release sites as [Ca2+]e was lowered, with a marked increase in silencing as the concentration decreased below the physiologic set point.
source: With this approach, we found glutamate exocytosis evoked by a single AP exhibited higher proportions of silencing at neurotransmitter release sites as [Ca2+]e was lowered, again demonstrating a marked increase in silencing as the concentration decreased below the physiologic set point (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: [Ca2+]e is an important regulator of presynaptic function, differentially dictating across synapses and neurons whether neurotransmitter will be released.
source: Thus, using these two fluorescent biosensors quantifying neurotransmitter handling under different stimulation regimes demonstrates that [Ca2+]e is an important regulator of presynaptic function, differentially dictating across synapses and neurons whether neurotransmitter will be released.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from Ca2+ influx, SV recycling, and glutamate release measurements.

claim: Agonism of the GABAB receptor (GABABR) lowers ICa by approximately 50% via interactions of the Gβγ subunit with presynaptic VGCCs.
source: One such canonical mechanism is the agonism of the GABAB receptor (GABABR), which lowers ICa by approximately 50% via interactions of the Gβγ subunit with presynaptic VGCCs (Mintz and Bean, 1993; Herlitze et al., 1996; Isaacson, 1998; Laviv et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mintz and Bean, 1993; Herlitze et al., 1996; Isaacson, 1998; Laviv et al., 2011.

claim: Agonizing GABABR at [Ca2+]e 1.2 mM caused an additional ~20% of terminals to become silent in both Ca2+ influx and SV recycling.
source: Consistent with our proposed mechanism, agonizing GABABR at [Ca2+]e 1.2 mM caused an additional ~20% of terminals to become silent in both Ca2+ influx and SV recycling (Figure 7D), similar to the proportional increase we observed decreasing [Ca2+]e to 0.8 mM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Agonism with baclofen in [Ca2+]e 2.0 mM led to a substantially lower increase in the proportion of silencing (7.6 ± 3.4% vs 20.5 ± 4.8%, p=0.017) compared to [Ca2+]e 1.2 mM.
source: However, agonism with baclofen in [Ca2+]e 2.0 mM led to a substantially lower increase in the proportion of silencing (7.6 ± 3.4% vs 20.5 ± 4.8%, p=0.017; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GPCR-mediated silencing was dependent on [Ca2+]e such that the impact was far greater operating at the physiologic [Ca2+]e.
source: Thus, GPCR-mediated silencing was dependent on [Ca2+]e such that the impact was far greater operating at the physiologic [Ca2+]e.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of baclofen effects at different [Ca2+]e.

claim: GPCR-mediated modulation acting presynaptically to decrease ICa can silence a substantial proportion of nerve terminals.
source: These results confirm that GPCR-mediated modulation acting presynaptically to decrease ICa can silence a substantial proportion of nerve terminals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the baclofen experiments.

claim: In responding terminals, baclofen was associated with ~40% decrease in Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: We observed that, in responding terminals, baclofen was associated with ~40% decrease in Δ[Ca2+]i.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from baclofen experiments.

claim: The ~40% decrease in Δ[Ca2+]i caused by baclofen led to an increase in the proportion of silent terminals from ~40 to 60%.
source: This decrement in Ca2+ influx led to an increase in the proportion of silent terminals from ~40 to 60%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from baclofen experiments.

claim: The difference in the degree of silencing and Δ[Ca2+]i caused by baclofen agreed excellently with results from decreasing [Ca2+]e 1.2–0.8 mM, supporting the conclusion that the effect of baclofen is mediated by decreasing presynaptic Ca2+ influx.
source: Notably, this difference in the degree of silencing and Δ[Ca2+]i agreed excellently with results from decreasing [Ca2+]e 1.2–0.8 mM, supporting the conclusion that the effect of baclofen is mediated by decreasing presynaptic Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of baclofen effects with [Ca2+]e manipulation.

claim: Baclofen caused substantially fewer terminals to become silent in [Ca2+]e 2.0 mM, highlighting the importance of physiologic [Ca2+]e in dictating synaptic function.
source: In addition, baclofen caused substantially fewer terminals to become silent in [Ca2+]e 2.0 mM, highlighting the importance of physiologic [Ca2+]e in dictating synaptic function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of baclofen effects at different [Ca2+]e.

claim: Chronic suppression of neuronal activity with tetrodotoxin (TTX) decreases the proportion of silent terminals.
source: Previous investigations indicate that silencing is a drastic form of synaptic homeostasis, as chronic suppression of neuronal activity with tetrodotoxin (TTX) decreases the proportion of silent terminals (Moulder et al., 2006) and increasing activity with chronic depolarization increases this proportion (Moulder et al., 2004; Moulder et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moulder et al., 2006.

claim: Increasing activity with chronic depolarization increases the proportion of silent terminals.
source: Previous investigations indicate that silencing is a drastic form of synaptic homeostasis, as chronic suppression of neuronal activity with tetrodotoxin (TTX) decreases the proportion of silent terminals (Moulder et al., 2006) and increasing activity with chronic depolarization increases this proportion (Moulder et al., 2004; Moulder et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moulder et al., 2004 and Moulder et al., 2006.

claim: Several intracellular signaling pathways have been identified to set the fraction of silent terminals, including those involving adenylyl cyclase, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, and calcineurin/cyclin-dependent kinase 5.
source: Several intracellular signaling pathways have been identified to set the fraction of silent terminals, including those involving adenylyl cyclase (Moulder et al., 2008), calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (Ninan and Arancio, 2004), and calcineurin/cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Kim and Ryan, 2010; Kim and Ryan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moulder et al., 2008; Ninan and Arancio, 2004; Kim and Ryan, 2010; Kim and Ryan, 2013.

claim: The disparate molecular pathways that converge on the regulation of synaptic silencing suggest that it is an important mode of plasticity for neurons in the CNS.
source: The disparate molecular pathways that converge on the regulation of synaptic silencing suggest that it is an important mode of plasticity for neurons in the CNS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of multiple pathways regulating silencing.

claim: In experiments investigating the impact of GPCR modulation, only a subset of GPCRs tested was able to alter silencing.
source: Notably, in experiments investigating the impact of GPCR modulation, only a subset of GPCRs tested was able to alter silencing (Crawford et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2011.

claim: The silencing caused by GABABR agonism was dependent on proteasome function in experiments utilizing 4 hr incubation with baclofen.
source: The silencing caused by GABABR agonism was dependent on proteasome function, and the authors concluded that protein degradation was necessary (Crawford et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2011.

claim: An acute effect of GABABR agonism independent of proteasomal activity may have been missed in previous experiments that used 4 hr incubation with baclofen.
source: However, these experiments utilized 4 hr incubation with baclofen, as opposed to 5 min here, so an acute effect of GABABR agonism independent of proteasomal activity may have been missed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the difference in experimental timescales.

claim: Silencing may have both proteasome-dependent and independent pathways, operating on slow (hours) or acute (<1 hr) time scales, respectively.
source: Indeed, silencing may have both proteasome-dependent and independent pathways, operating on slow (hours) or acute (<1 hr) time scales, respectively (Crawford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2012.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of proteasome function prevents depolarization-induced silencing.
source: Moreover, pharmacologic inhibition of proteasome function prevents depolarization-induced silencing, so the effect of proteasome inhibition may not be specific to GABABR agonism (Jiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2010.

claim: The results suggest a separate, rapid mechanism by which nerve terminals can be silenced, adding to the diversity of pathways by which this form of plasticity is achieved.
source: Thus, our results suggest a separate, rapid mechanism by which nerve terminals can be silenced, adding to the diversity of pathways by which this form of plasticity is achieved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the acute timescale of silencing observed in the experiments.

claim: The definition of silent terminals as those with ΔF below one standard deviation of pre-stimulus fluorescence agrees well with other approaches used.
source: We classified terminals for which the ΔF of Ca2+ entry falls below one standard deviation of pre-stimulus fluorescence as silent. This previously used definition agrees well with the other approaches used (Moulder et al., 2008; Moulder et al., 2004; Moulder et al., 2006; Crawford et al., 2011; Crawford et al., 2012; Hogins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies using similar definitions.

claim: Given that Ca2+ influx is itself non-linearly related to SV exocytosis, even if Ca2+ entry has only been inhibited to undetectable levels, this level would lead to even rarer neurotransmitter release.
source: Given that Ca2+ influx is itself non-linearly related to SV exocytosis, even if Ca2+ entry has only been inhibited to undetectable levels, this level would lead to even rarer neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known cooperative relationship between Ca2+ and exocytosis.

claim: The sub-proportional relationship of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e and the heterogeneous changes of individual nerve terminals to changes in [Ca2+]e refutes the simple biophysical model of the relationship of Ca2+ influx to [Ca2+]e.
source: The sub-proportional relationship of Δ[Ca2+]i to [Ca2+]e and the heterogeneous changes of individual nerve terminals to changes in [Ca2+]e refutes the simple biophysical model of the relationship of Ca2+ influx to [Ca2+]e.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations that contradict the simple model.

claim: The results support nerve terminal specificity in the propensity to have presynaptic function diminished by perturbations that lower the driving force for Ca2+ entry.
source: Rather, our results support nerve terminal specificity in the propensity to have presynaptic function diminished by perturbations that lower the driving force for Ca2+ entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the heterogeneous responses of terminals to [Ca2+]e changes.

claim: Models of the synapse that account for its limited volume and restriction of diffusion have predicted that drastic reductions of local [Ca2+]e may occur during repetitive presynaptic firing.
source: Although [Ca2+] of the CSF is tightly regulated globally (Forsberg et al., 2019; Jones and Keep, 1988; Barkai and Meltzer, 1982), models of the synapse that account for its limited volume and restriction of diffusion have predicted that drastic reductions of local [Ca2+]e may occur during repetitive presynaptic firing (Egelman and Montague, 1999; King et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egelman and Montague, 1999 and King et al., 2001.

claim: [Ca2+] of the CSF is tightly regulated globally.
source: Although [Ca2+] of the CSF is tightly regulated globally (Forsberg et al., 2019; Jones and Keep, 1988; Barkai and Meltzer, 1982), models of the synapse that account for its limited volume and restriction of diffusion have predicted that drastic reductions of local [Ca2+]e may occur during repetitive presynaptic firing (Egelman and Montague, 1999; King et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Forsberg et al., 2019; Jones and Keep, 1988; Barkai and Meltzer, 1982.

claim: The phenomenon of [Ca2+]e-mediated silencing may be important in vivo as a homeostatic mechanism to prevent excessive or runaway synaptic activity.
source: Thus, the phenomenon we observed may be important in vivo as a homeostatic mechanism to prevent excessive or runaway synaptic activity (Stringer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about the potential in vivo function, supported by citation to Stringer et al., 2007.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Hodgkin and Katz, 1949 and Yu et al., 2012.
